extraction.text:
This document outlines a partnership framework for advancing equity across the Minnesota Department of Human Services (DHS) through the One DHS People, Access and Culture Program. As the Equity & Inclusion Operations Consultant within the Disability Services Division (DSD), I bring a specific lens—disability equity—to this broader agency-wide effort. But this work cannot and should not happen in isolation.

The One DHS People, Access and Culture Program is the vehicle through which we can coordinate equity efforts across all administrations, avoid duplication, share resources, and ensure that our collective impact is greater than the sum of our parts. This framework is designed to suggest recommendations, offer tools, and support the work of the Office of Employee Culture, Equity Directors, Equity Specialists, and all interested parties who are committed to building a more equitable DHS.

This is not a decision memo. It is an invitation to partnership.

---

Guiding Principles for the One DHS Equity Partnership

Principle What It Means in Practice
Equity is Everyone's Work Equity is not the responsibility of a single office or role. It is embedded in every administration, every program, and every decision.
We Build on Existing Infrastructure The Office of Employee Culture, Equity Directors, and Equity Specialists are the backbone of this work. We amplify their capacity, not duplicate their efforts.
We Center Lived Experience People with disabilities, BIPOC communities, immigrants, LGBTQ+ individuals, and other marginalized groups are the experts. They are compensated partners, not passive recipients.
We Follow the Data Every recommendation is tied to measurable outcomes, disaggregated by race, ethnicity, language, disability, gender identity, sexual orientation, and geography.
We Move at the Speed of Trust Systemic change is slow. We celebrate incremental wins while maintaining urgency on long-term transformation.
We Work in Partnership This is a collaborative effort across all DHS administrations, counties, tribes, providers, and community organizations.

---

Domain 1: Improving Workplace Culture Across DHS

Partners: Office of Employee Culture, Administration Equity Directors, Equity Specialists, HR Business Partners, Union Representatives, Employee Resource Groups

The Challenge: DHS employees from marginalized communities report higher rates of burnout, lower promotion rates, and experiences of microaggressions and exclusion. A toxic or unwelcoming workplace culture undermines service delivery and drives talent away from the agency.

Suggested Recommendations & Actions

1.1 Conduct an Agency-Wide Employee Equity Climate Assessment

· Action: Partner with the Office of Employee Culture to design and administer a comprehensive, anonymous climate survey across all DHS administrations, disaggregated by race, ethnicity, gender identity, disability status, sexual orientation, job classification, and administration.
· A Tool We Can Use: An employee climate survey instrument template—a structured questionnaire designed to measure belonging, psychological safety, and experiences of inclusion or exclusion across different employee groups, along with an analysis framework and facilitation guides for post-survey listening sessions.
· Outcome: A baseline data set identifying where belonging, psychological safety, and advancement opportunities diverge across employee groups agency-wide.

1.2 Establish a Cross-Administration Equity Learning Community

· Action: Convene Equity Directors, Equity Specialists, and interested staff from all DHS administrations on a regular basis to share best practices, troubleshoot challenges, coordinate initiatives, and build collective knowledge.
· A Tool We Can Use: A Learning Community Charter—a governance document that outlines membership criteria, meeting cadence, agenda templates, and knowledge-sharing protocols to ensure consistent and productive collaboration.
· Outcome: A connected network of equity practitioners across DHS who can support each other and avoid duplicating efforts.

1.3 Audit Hiring, Promotion, and Retention Data Across Administrations

· Action: Work with HR Business Partners and the Office of Employee Culture to conduct a disaggregated analysis of the full employee lifecycle across all DHS administrations: applicant pool demographics, interview selection rates, hire rates, promotion velocity, and exit interview themes by identity group and administration.
· A Tool We Can Use: A Lifecycle Equity Dashboard—an interactive data visualization template that tracks where BIPOC, LGBTQ+, and disabled employees enter, advance, or exit the employment pipeline, with filters to view data by administration.
· Outcome: Identification of specific bottleneck stages where bias or structural barriers are most acute, both agency-wide and within specific administrations.

1.4 Establish Employee Resource Group (ERG) Infrastructure with Real Authority

· Action: Support the Office of Employee Culture in formalizing ERGs as strategic partners, not social clubs. ERG leaders should have dedicated time, budget, and a direct line to executive leadership across all administrations.
· A Tool We Can Use: An ERG Charter Template—a customizable document that defines an ERG's mission, membership, leadership structure, budget authority, and reporting relationships, along with an Executive Sponsor Role Description that clarifies expectations and accountability.
· Outcome: ERGs that can surface workplace concerns, inform policy development, and provide peer support without burning out their leaders.

1.5 Develop a Structured Mentorship and Sponsorship Program Across DHS

· Action: Create a program that pairs high-potential BIPOC, LGBTQ+, and disabled employees with senior leaders across administrations who can advocate for their advancement (sponsorship, not just advice).
· A Tool We Can Use: A Sponsorship Playbook—a training guide that teaches senior leaders the difference between mentorship and sponsorship, and provides practical strategies for using their influence to advance equity in promotions and professional development.
· Outcome: Increased representation of marginalized groups in supervisory and executive roles across all DHS administrations.

1.6 Embed Equity Competencies into Performance Evaluations Agency-Wide

· Action: Partner with HR and the Office of Employee Culture to revise performance evaluation rubrics across all DHS administrations to include measurable equity competencies for all supervisors and managers.
· A Tool We Can Use: An Equity Competency Scoring Guide—a resource that provides sample competency language and defines what "meets expectations," "exceeds expectations," and "needs development" looks like for equity-focused leadership.
· Outcome: Accountability for equity is built into the formal performance management system across the entire agency.

---

Domain 2: Equitable Access to DHS Programs and Services

Partners: Administration Equity Directors, Equity Specialists, Program Managers, Data Analytics Unit, Community Engagement Specialists, County and Tribal Partners, Community-Based Organizations

The Challenge: DHS programs—Medicaid, SNAP, disability waivers, behavioral health services, aging services—do not reach all eligible Minnesotans equally. Administrative burden, language barriers, geographic deserts, and cultural disconnects create disparate access and outcomes.

Suggested Recommendations & Actions

2.1 Launch an Agency-Wide "Equity Impact Assessment" (EIA) Protocol

· Action: Before any new policy, waiver amendment, RFP, or system change is approved across any DHS administration, it must undergo an EIA. The EIA asks: Who will be negatively impacted? What data informed this decision? Have affected communities been consulted? What mitigation strategies are in place?
· A Tool We Can Use: An Equity Impact Assessment Toolkit—a set of resources including a user-friendly EIA template, scoring rubric, and decision-tree flowchart that guides program managers through evaluating the equity implications of proposed changes before they are approved.
· Outcome: Equity is considered at the front end of policy design across all DHS administrations, not retrofitted after harm has occurred.

2.2 Conduct Administrative Burden Audits on High-Touch Programs

· Action: For SNAP, MFIP, Medical Assistance, disability waiver applications, and other high-touch programs, map every step a client must complete. Identify where applicants drop off, which steps cause the most confusion, and which requirements disproportionately burden people with limited English proficiency, disabilities, or caregiving responsibilities.
· A Tool We Can Use: A Burden Mapping Template—a step-by-step visual mapping tool that documents every client touchpoint in an application or renewal process, paired with a Simplification Checklist that provides plain-language standards and redundancy elimination guidelines.
· Outcome: Shorter, simpler applications; reduced churn; increased enrollment among eligible but unserved populations across all DHS programs.

2.3 Standardize Language Access Across the Agency

· Action: Audit current language access practices across all DHS administrations. Ensure that a client's preferred language follows them through every DHS touchpoint—from initial application to ongoing case management to appeals.
· A Tool We Can Use: A Language Access Protocol Toolkit—a comprehensive resource containing staff training modules, signage templates, data field specifications for tracking language preference, and a vendor quality scorecard for evaluating translation and interpretation services.
· Outcome: No client is denied services or experiences adverse outcomes because of language barriers, regardless of which DHS program they access.

2.4 Redesign Contract and RFP Language for Equity Accountability

· Action: Work with Equity Directors and the procurement team to revise standard contract boilerplate across all DHS administrations. Replace vague "diversity and inclusion" statements with binding, measurable equity requirements.
· A Tool We Can Use: A Contract Language Library—a searchable digital collection of model equity clauses for RFPs, contracts, and MOUs that includes disaggregated data reporting requirements, community engagement mandates, workforce equity standards, and financial consequences for non-performance.
· Outcome: Vendors, MCOs, county partners, and providers across all DHS programs are held accountable for equitable service delivery.

2.5 Expand Culturally Specific Provider Networks Across All Services

· Action: Identify barriers that prevent BIPOC-owned clinics, Indigenous healers, immigrant-serving organizations, disability service providers, and peer-run services from becoming DHS-certified providers. Streamline credentialing, offer billing technical assistance, and create a dedicated liaison.
· A Tool We Can Use: A Provider Onboarding Gap Analysis Template—a diagnostic tool that identifies specific barriers preventing culturally specific organizations from becoming DHS-certified providers, paired with a Technical Assistance Curriculum tailored to community-based organizations.
· Outcome: A more diverse provider network across all DHS programs that reflects the communities DHS serves.

2.6 Implement Community Co-Design Protocols Agency-Wide

· Action: Move beyond listening sessions across all DHS administrations. Compensate community members with lived experience to serve as active design partners on policy changes, program redesigns, and system improvements.
· A Tool We Can Use: A Community Co-Design Playbook—a practical guide that includes recruitment strategies, compensation guidelines, facilitation agendas, and feedback loop mechanisms for meaningfully engaging community members as design partners.
· Outcome: Policies and programs across all DHS administrations that are shaped by the people they are meant to serve, not just informed by them.

---

Domain 3: Addressing Systemic Challenges and Inequities

Partners: Executive Leadership, Office of Employee Culture, Administration Equity Directors, Equity Specialists, Data Analytics Unit, Legislative Affairs, Tribal Relations, County Partners

The Challenge: Systemic inequities are not the result of individual bias alone; they are embedded in funding formulas, data collection practices, and decision-making structures across all DHS administrations. Addressing them requires structural change at the highest levels.

Suggested Recommendations & Actions

3.1 Build an Agency-Wide Equity Data Infrastructure

· Action: Partner with the Data Analytics Unit and Equity Specialists across administrations to standardize race, ethnicity, language, disability, sexual orientation, and gender identity data collection across all DHS systems. Ensure data is linkable across programs to identify cross-cutting disparities.
· A Tool We Can Use: A Data Governance for Equity Framework—a structured guide that addresses privacy considerations, tribal data sovereignty, and responsible use protocols, along with templates for data-sharing agreements with counties, tribes, and community partners.
· Outcome: DHS has the analytic capacity to identify, track, and address disparities in real time across all administrations.

3.2 Establish a Tribal Consultation and Sovereignty Protocol

· Action: Formalize consultation processes with the 11 Tribal nations in Minnesota across all DHS administrations. Ensure that data collection, program design, and policy decisions affecting American Indian communities are made with tribal consent and leadership.
· A Tool We Can Use: A Tribal Consultation Checklist—an operational guide for government-to-government engagement that outlines required consultation steps, along with Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) Templates that formalize relationships with Tribal nations.
· Outcome: DHS policies and programs across all administrations respect tribal sovereignty and contribute to closing disparities for American Indian communities.

3.3 Conduct a Funding Equity Analysis Across Administrations

· Action: Analyze how DHS allocates resources across counties, providers, and programs. Identify whether funding formulas disadvantage rural communities, BIPOC-concentrated urban areas, or under-resourced regions.
· A Tool We Can Use: A Funding Equity Mapping Tool—an interactive data visualization resource that overlays demographic data with funding distribution to reveal geographic and demographic disparities in resource allocation.
· Outcome: Data-driven advocacy for budget adjustments that target resources to communities with the greatest need across all DHS programs.

3.4 Develop an Agency-Wide Equity Learning and Development Curriculum

· Action: Move beyond one-off diversity trainings across all DHS administrations. Create a tiered curriculum that builds equity competencies at all levels: foundational awareness for all staff, advanced skills for supervisors, and strategic leadership for executives.
· A Tool We Can Use: An Equity Curriculum Map—a structured planning document that outlines learning objectives, module outlines, and evaluation metrics for a tiered equity education program, along with recommendations for external trainers and internal facilitators.
· Outcome: A workforce across all DHS administrations that has the knowledge, skills, and motivation to advance equity in their daily work.

3.5 Create an Agency-Wide Equity Accountability Dashboard and Reporting Cadence

· Action: Publish a public-facing dashboard that tracks progress on key equity indicators across all DHS administrations: workforce representation, promotion rates, service access disparities, and outcome gaps by race, language, disability, and geography.
· A Tool We Can Use: An Equity Accountability Dashboard—a public-facing progress tracker with pre-designed wireframes, indicator definitions, and a reporting calendar template for regular updates to the legislature and the public.
· Outcome: Transparency and accountability. The public, the legislature, and DHS staff can see where progress is happening and where it is stalled across the entire agency.

3.6 Establish a Standing DHS Equity Council

· Action: Formalize a standing council of Equity Directors and Equity Specialists from each administration, co-chaired by the Office of Employee Culture, with a direct line to the Commissioner. This council reviews EIA findings, shares best practices, coordinates cross-cutting initiatives, and advises on budget and policy decisions.
· A Tool We Can Use: A DHS Equity Council Charter—a governance document that defines membership criteria, meeting cadence, decision-making authority, and escalation pathways for institutionalizing equity as a core governance function.
· Outcome: Equity is institutionalized as a core governance function across all DHS administrations, not a siloed initiative.

---

Resources and Tools for Advancing Equity Writ Large

The following resources will be developed and made available to all DHS staff, Equity Directors, Equity Specialists, and partners through the One DHS People, Access and Culture Program:

Resource What It Is and What It Is Used For
Equity Impact Assessment (EIA) Toolkit A set of resources—including a template, scoring rubric, and decision-tree—used to evaluate the equity implications of proposed policies, waivers, RFPs, or system changes before they are approved.
Language Access Protocol Toolkit A comprehensive resource with staff training modules, signage templates, and data field specifications used to ensure clients' language preferences are consistently tracked and honored across all DHS touchpoints.
Community Co-Design Playbook A practical guide with recruitment, compensation, facilitation, and feedback loop strategies used to meaningfully engage community members with lived experience as active design partners.
Lifecycle Equity Dashboard An interactive data visualization template used to track where BIPOC, LGBTQ+, and disabled employees enter, advance, or exit the employment pipeline across DHS administrations.
Administrative Burden Mapping Template A step-by-step visual mapping tool used to document every client touchpoint in an application or renewal process and identify steps that cause confusion or drop-off.
Sponsorship Playbook A training guide used to teach senior leaders how to advocate for the advancement of marginalized staff using their political capital and influence.
Equity Curriculum Map A structured planning document used to outline learning objectives, module outlines, and evaluation metrics for a tiered equity education program across all staff levels.
Tribal Consultation Checklist An operational guide used to ensure government-to-government engagement with Tribal nations follows required consultation steps and respects tribal sovereignty.
Funding Equity Mapping Tool An interactive data visualization resource used to overlay demographic data with funding distribution to reveal geographic and demographic disparities in resource allocation.
Contract Language Library A searchable digital collection of model equity clauses used to insert binding, measurable equity requirements into RFPs, contracts, and MOUs.
Equity Accountability Dashboard A public-facing progress tracker used to monitor and report on key equity indicators—workforce representation, service access, and outcome gaps—to the legislature and the public.
Learning Community Charter A governance document used to define membership, meeting cadence, and knowledge-sharing protocols for cross-administration equity collaboration.
DHS Equity Council Charter A governance document used to formalize a standing council of Equity Directors and Specialists with decision-making authority and a direct line to the Commissioner.
Provider Onboarding Gap Analysis Template A diagnostic tool used to identify specific barriers preventing culturally specific organizations from becoming DHS-certified providers.
Employee Climate Survey Instrument A structured questionnaire used to measure belonging, psychological safety, and experiences of inclusion or exclusion across different employee groups.
Equity Competency Scoring Guide A resource used to define what "meets expectations," "exceeds expectations," and "needs development" looks like for equity-focused leadership in performance evaluations.
Data Governance for Equity Framework A structured guide used to address privacy, tribal data sovereignty, and responsible use protocols when collecting and sharing disaggregated equity data.
